title: Google Docs
seoTitle: Design a Collaborative Editor Like Google Docs
description: Design Google Docs — real-time collaborative editing with operational transformation or CRDTs, WebSocket sessions, presence and scalable document storage.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: Understanding the Problem

blocks.title: What is Google Docs?
blocks.text: Google Docs is a browser-based word processor where many people can edit the same document at the same time and see each other's changes and cursors live.
Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Users should be able to create a document.
Multiple users should be able to edit the same document concurrently.
Users should see other users' changes in real time.
Users should see the cursor positions and presence of other editors.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):

items: Offline editing and full version history.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

blocks.text: Non-Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Edits should propagate to other collaborators with low latency (< 100ms).
All collaborators must converge to the same document state (eventual consistency with convergence).
The system should scale to millions of concurrent documents, with up to ~100 concurrent editors per document.
Documents must be durable — no acknowledged edit is ever lost.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):

items: Documents larger than a few MB.

blocks.text: The Set Up
Planning the Approach

The central challenge is **concurrent edits to the same text**. If two users insert at position 5 at the same time, naively applying both produces different documents on each screen. We need an algorithm that guarantees convergence, plus an architecture that routes all editors of a document together.
Defining the Core Entities

items: **Document**: id, title, and its current content (or a snapshot plus operations).
**Edit (Operation)**: an insert or delete at a position, with the document version it was based on.
**Cursor / Presence**: a user's position and selection in a document.
**Editor**: a user connected to a document.

blocks.text: API or System Interface
Creating a document is plain REST:
Editing happens over a WebSocket, because changes flow both ways continuously:
High-Level Design
1) Users should be able to create a document
A **Document Metadata Service** creates the document record and an empty content snapshot.
2) Users should be able to edit concurrently and see changes in real time

Clients connect to a **Document Service** over WebSockets. Every edit is sent to the server, which orders it, transforms it against concurrent edits, persists it and broadcasts it to the other connected editors.
3) Users should see cursors and presence

Cursor updates are sent over the same WebSocket but are **ephemeral**: the server broadcasts them to other editors and keeps them in memory only. Losing a cursor update is harmless; the next one replaces it.
Potential Deep Dives
1) How do we make concurrent edits converge?

blocks.title: Last write wins on the whole document

approach.text: Each client sends the full document; the latest save overwrites.

challenges.text: Concurrent edits silently erase each other. Completely unusable for real-time collaboration.

blocks.title: Operational Transformation (OT) with a central server

approach.text: Clients send operations tagged with the version they were based on. The server holds the authoritative sequence: if an incoming op is based on an older version, it is **transformed** against every op applied since — e.g. an insert at position 5 is shifted to 7 if someone else inserted 2 characters before it. The transformed op gets the next version number and is broadcast. Clients similarly transform incoming ops against their own pending, unacknowledged ops.

challenges.text: OT requires a single ordering authority per document, and transformation functions are subtle to get right (especially with rich text). It's what Google Docs actually uses.

approach.text: Use a Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (e.g. Yjs, Automerge) where every character has a unique, ordered identifier. Operations commute, so replicas converge regardless of the order they apply ops — no central transformation needed, which also enables offline and peer-to-peer editing.

challenges.text: CRDT metadata (identifiers and tombstones for deleted characters) can make documents larger, and garbage-collecting it is complex. A server is still useful for persistence and fan-out.

blocks.text: 2) How do we route all editors of a document to the same server?

OT needs one server to order each document's operations. Use **consistent hashing on docId** so every client for a document connects to the same Document Service instance. A coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd) holds the ring; on scale-out or failure, documents move to their new owner, which loads the latest snapshot plus subsequent ops before accepting edits.
If two servers believe they own the same document (split brain), they will assign conflicting versions. Ownership needs leases with fencing tokens so a stale owner's writes are rejected.
3) How do we store documents durably and load them quickly?

approach.text: Append every op to a log keyed by `(docId, version)`; replay to build the document.

challenges.text: Opening a document with a million edits means replaying a million ops.

approach.text: Persist each op durably before acknowledging it (so no edit is lost), and periodically write a **snapshot** of the full document at version N. Loading a document reads the latest snapshot and replays only the ops after it. Old ops can be archived or deleted once covered by a snapshot.

challenges.text: Snapshotting must not block editing — do it asynchronously from the op log.

blocks.text: Final Design

quiz.question: What problem do OT and CRDTs solve?
options: Making concurrent edits converge to the same document
quiz.explanation: Both guarantee all replicas end up identical even when users edit simultaneously.

quiz.question: Why are all editors of a document routed to the same server in an OT design?
options: OT needs a single authority to order operations
quiz.explanation: One owner assigns versions and transforms ops, so routing by docId (consistent hashing) is used.

quiz.question: How do snapshots help document loading?
options: You replay only ops after the latest snapshot instead of the full history
They replace the op log entirely
quiz.explanation: Snapshots bound replay cost no matter how long the edit history grows.

quiz.question: Why can cursor positions be kept only in memory?
options: They are ephemeral — a lost update is replaced by the next one
quiz.explanation: Presence doesn't need durability; persisting it would only add load.
